patient_information: A 40-year-old Thai woman, married, housewife, who has lived in Germany for the past 13 years.
chief_complaint: Severe headache for the past 8 days.
history_of_present_illness: The headache was of gradual onset, unresponsive to painkillers, and not associated with fever, chills, visual problems, limb weakness, or memory problems; a prior CT scan of her brain and blood count were reported as normal.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Ten days prior to presentation, she returned from a 4-week journey to north-east Thailand, where she consumed traditional regional dishes including freshwater fish, seafood, snails, and frogs, and her brother-in-law, who shared these meals, also developed a severe headache.
physical_exam: On examination, she is afebrile, with a supple neck, negative Lasègue's sign, equal and reactive pupils, no cranial nerve palsies, and an unremarkable neurological examination, including higher cortical functions; there is no rash, oral thrush, subcutaneous swellings, lymphadenopathy, and cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams are normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: Initial blood tests revealed WBC 12.3 x 10^9/L, Eosinophils 2.34 x 10^9/L, Haemoglobin 11.7 mg/dL, MCV 70 fL, Platelets 330 x 10^9/L, ESR 20 mm/h, IgE 944 U/mL, Creatinine 62 µmol/L, ALT 28 U/L, GGT 35 U/L, and C-reactive protein <5 mg/L; a lumbar puncture showed CSF with 1877 leukocytes/µL (42% eosinophils, 39% lymphocytes, 18% monocytes, 1% neutrophils), elevated protein 1.59 g/L, glucose 1.85 mmol/L, and elevated opening pressure 34 cmH2O; CSF microscopy, Ziehl-Neelsen stain, cryptococcal antigen, and cultures were negative, as were urine and stool microscopy; Taenia solium, Fasciola hepatica, Paragonimus serologies were negative, Toxocara canis serology was weakly positive, and HIV serology was negative; after discharge, Western Blot showed specific antibodies against 31kD Angiostrongylus cantonensis antigen.
differential_diagnosis: Food-borne parasitic infection of the meninges, fungal meningitis (Coccidioides immitis), lymphoma, eosinophilic leukaemia, sarcoid, and idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient underwent serial lumbar punctures to relieve headache and received iron tablets for mild microcytic anaemia; she was discharged significantly improved after a 1-week hospital stay, and no further specific treatment was prescribed after serology confirmed Angiostrongylus cantonensis, with full recovery and normal peripheral eosinophil count at 4-week follow-up.
final_diagnosis: Eosinophilic Meningitis due to Angiostrongylus cantonensis infection.
